message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Parallel graphics rendering – processes many similar operations at once. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32), each highly optimized for complex control flow, branching, and low latency. | Hundreds or thousands of simpler cores, optimized for throughput on identical or very similar tasks. |
| **Execution model** | Serial or lightly parallel; each core can run a single thread with sophisticated pipelines, branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution. | SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) – one instruction executed simultaneously across many data elements. |
| **Memory hierarchy** | Large caches per core, deep memory hierarchy, high bandwidth per core. | Smaller per‑core caches, but massive shared memory and high aggregate bandwidth. |
| **Typical workloads** | Operating system services, database queries, web servers, general software. | Rendering 3D graphics, video encoding/decoding, scientific simulations, machine learning inference/training. |
| **Programming model** | Traditional sequential code, multithreading with synchronization primitives. | Data‑parallel programming (CUDA, OpenCL, Vulkan compute shaders). |
| **Power & cost** | More power‑hungry per core, higher cost per core. | Lower power per core, cheaper per core, but overall cost depends on total number of cores. |

In short, CPUs excel at tasks that require complex decision making and low latency, while GPUs shine when you can break a problem into many identical, independent operations that can be processed in parallel.
